description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
_**Output 1: Participants understand and apply the principles of agro-business plan development**_. During the TMT workshop activities, participants were introduced to a business modeling card game where groups of people can identify key components of the critical stakeholder environment of an enterprise, discuss the nature and extent of these relations and draw management plans to manage this environment in order to make the enterprise to survive and grow. After some instruction by the TMT teachers, participants set out in subgroups to apply the card game for the mechanized seed potato farm in Burundi. Interestingly the participants who are of the majority staff of government agencies that are relevant for the seed potato sector in Burundi, also critically discussed the service delivery of their own institutes, seen from the perspective of the agro-entrepreneur. Apparently, this game effectively switched their perspective, as before, in statements about the potato sector, there was mainly mention of the importance of the regulations of these agencies to which entrepreneurs just had to adhere..
_**Output 2: Participants able to assess investment needs for different business development scenarios**_. As a follow-up to the business model game the subgroups had to assess the investment needs of their business models and specify timing, intensity and nature of the investments. The subgroups thereafter presented in a plenary session their findings, and were requested to comment upon each others' results. This resulted in interesting discussions about business development possibilities and alternatives in the Burundian agro-sector. Three scenarios for business development of the seed potato enterprise are subsequently developed in plenary, including their investment needs.
_**Output 3: Participants can design a practical multi-year enterprise cash flow analysis and undertake a financing needs assessment**_. As described in this report's chapter 3 "Bottlenecks, deviations and possible adjustments", the training encountered the complication that a sizable part of the participants (mainly the participants representing government agencies) had no affinity with business financing, cash flows, etcetera. To adapt to that finding, this part related to output 3 was undertaken by the TMT participants from private sector and from the Investment Development Agency ADB. They first choose the most likely business development scenario for the seed potato farm and then set out to determine its revenue and costs, as well its investments, in the framework of a 10-year cashflow forecast. From the emerging cumulative cash flow calculations the specific financing needs for investments and the operational exploitations of the farm components were calculated. To save time, most components of the cash flow forecast model were already pre-set, based on a cash flow model of a similar seed potato farm in Uganda.
**Output 4: Participants understand the function and purpose of different forms of finance (equity, loans, secured loans, conditional grants, credit etc.).** After having set up the cash flow forecast model (which cost the participants quite some time and discussion energy) It was easy to import in the model the different financing forms and see their effects on the financial well-being of the enterprise on the short and medium term. By applying it in the model and playing around with it, participants also gained a good understanding of the use and effects of these different finance forms.
_**Output 5: Participants able to identify finance sources and suppliers, and their conditions**_. In this part of the course, the participants with less affinity with business finance, the government agencies staff, again joined to identify finance sources, finance suppliers and their financing conditions. Here an interesting dichotomy developed between the two groups of participants. The government staff had done their homework and listed the development funds (grants and co-financing) from national, bilateral and multilateral agencies. The private sector participants, however, took another approach. For them, the exercises with business finance had been so super realistic that they came up with existing agricultural development networks whom they had effectively approached whether these could be launching customers for the new seed potato enterprise. Also, they came up with Burundian private investors with whom they had discussed the business case of the envisaged seed potato enterprise and who subsequently showed interest to invest in it. Their motto: "Why waste your time with applying for subsidies or loans for a profitable business, while there are people who can invest in it tomorrow and get your business going by next week?" This was an amazing outcome that the organizers of this TMT could not possibly have been hoping for...
_**Output 6: Elaborate a finance application for the most relevant finance providers/facilities, prepare a finance negotiation**_. In the discussion s about the finance options for the seed potato farm, everyone agreed, including the TMT participants from government agencies, that pursuing the investment of a launching customer and some private investors would be the best finance application option on the short term to work out. And, the participants agreed after long discussions, if the seed potato enterprise would would be up and running with acquired first customers and investors providing the company's starting capital, it would also be in a better position to apply for a co-financing from an institutional funding agency. So subsequently, the business plan was further developed to better suit negotiations with the launching customer and the investors. As of the time of this TMT reporting, the negotiations with these parties actually started and the perspectives are quite good.
_**Output 7: Participants able to apply the basics of design of training modules in practical agro-finance.**_ The TMT participants discussed whether the business development trajectory that they themselves had undergone would be typical for any other business development exercise in real life. It was decided that in any case the example from this TMT would be interesting to use in an enterprise financing training module in the envisaged seed potato learning farm. The main components of the training module were identified by the TMT course participants and most of them indicated that they would be happy to be involved in the detailed formulation and administering of the training module in future, once the seed potato learning will have effectively been set up.
